content: HCLS1-associated protein X-1, encoded by the HAX1 gene in humans, is a protein that interacts with HS1, a substrate of Src family tyrosine kinases. This protein also binds to the product of the PKD2 gene, mutations of which are implicated in autosomal-dominant polycystic kidney disease. Additionally, it interacts with cortactin, a protein that binds to filamentous actin (F-actin). While it was previously believed that the HAX1 protein is predominantly localized in the mitochondria, more recent research has demonstrated its presence in the cell body. Two distinct transcript variants of the HAX1 gene, encoding different isoforms of the protein, have been identified. Furthermore, in 2015, studies confirmed the localization of the HAX1 protein to P-bodies, which are cytoplasmic structures involved in mRNA regulation and decay. Homozygous mutations in the HAX1 gene are associated with autosomal recessive severe congenital neutropenia, also referred to as Kostmann syndrome. This condition is characterized by a profound deficiency of neutrophils, a type of white blood cell essential for immune defense. The HAX1 protein has been shown to interact with interleukin-1 alpha (IL1A). Additionally, it has been demonstrated to bind to the 3' untranslated regions (UTRs) of transcripts for vimentin, an intermediate filament protein, and DNA polymerase beta, an enzyme involved in DNA repair.
